prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred third name from Knudsen to Mojsov, and I want to say why in terms of principle rather than head-count. The chair asked us to decide what the prize is for before choosing the name. Our round-1 exchange shows that the disagreement was never about the science of GLP-1, which all six of us rank first on an unusually complete arc from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, through receptor biology, to replicated outcome-trial benefit in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. It was about which step the citation should anchor. My own round-1 argument was that acylation-based half-life extension is what turned the physiology into a medicine, and I still believe that is a real scientific achievement. But the principle I can defend in public is that this prize rewards the discovery that opened the field, and that the therapy is the evidence of its consequence. On that principle the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form are the discovery, and the long-acting analogues are a development that rests on it. A citation anchored in physiology also does not read as honouring a commercial product, which was the most serious external risk in the configuration I proposed in round 1. Holst (secretion, processing and insulinotropic action) and Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology, receptor action and translational rationale) are fixed for me, as they are for all six of us. The citation says 'its active form' and does not use the word 'first', so it recognises Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide without ruling on priority against Habener or others.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I have not made them disappear by changing my ballot. Knudsen is left out, and the citation, although it says incretin-based treatment was made possible, does not name the people who made the peptide usable once daily and then once weekly. A critic can say that this honours the hormone and skips the drug. Mojsov's priority for the active form is disputed in the literature, Habener is not on the supplied list, and I cannot verify the dispute from the record in front of us, so including her still rests on a claim that nobody here has independently checked. I should also be honest that the evidence for her is no stronger now than it was in round 1. What has changed is how I weigh the competing risks under a stated principle, not what we know. Finally, a one-part prize with three names leaves no room for any other achievement, and long-term durability and safety of incretin therapy in obesity are still accruing, although I do not think either point affects the ranking.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio under a discovery-centred citation, says the prize should stay anchored in physiology, and worries that the outcome is so far ahead of other candidates that credit allocation may not be tested hard enough.
responses.response: Your last point is the one I take most seriously, and it is why I tried to test my own position before moving. I think we have now tested it: the two groups have stated opposing principles, and neither has shown the other's factual premise to be wrong. Where I move toward you is on the principle. A physiology-anchored citation is more defensible than the version I proposed in round 1, because it does not depend on arguing that an industrial development step is itself a discovery. Where I still differ is on the weight of Knudsen's work. I do not accept the description of her contribution as secondary, and I would not want the citation to imply that the therapy arrived on its own. That is why I would keep the wording that incretin treatment was made possible, rather than drop the clinical consequence altogether. If you and I are both uncertain about Mojsov's priority, the honest position is to say so and to word the citation around the identification of the active form, not around who was first.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, keeps Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and says he would move if the committee judges peptide identification to be more decisive, while noting that he has not verified the priority dispute around Mojsov.
responses.response: We agreed in round 1, and I am now leaving that pairing, so I owe you a direct reason. You are right that a prize that stops at the hormone leaves the therapeutic half unrecognised, and I do not dismiss that. My reason for moving is that the objection to our trio, that it could read as a prize for a product and as an exclusion of Mojsov by default, turned out to be harder to answer than the objection to the other trio. A citation that names the development of long-acting agonists makes the commercial reading difficult to avoid, and the committee would then have to explain why one industrial team is named and the work on the active peptide is not. I also note that your own statement says you have not verified the priority question, so my change of mind does not depend on resolving it. If you still think the development step is the more decisive one, I would like you to say what evidence in the supplied record shows that, because I have not found any that separates the two on science alone.

responses.point: El Manira describes Knudsen's work as the engineering step rather than the discovery, favours a three-name prize built around the physiology and active form of GLP-1, and asks whether the committee would accept a prize that omits the long-acting analogues.
responses.response: In round 1 I disagreed with your description of the analogue as engineering, and I still think it understates the work. Converting a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly medicine required insight into albumin binding and acylation, and the outcome trials depend on it. Still, your underlying argument is about the type of contribution the prize rewards, and on that I now agree with you more than I did. I do not need to call acylation trivial to say that it is a development built on the discovery. Your question is whether the committee would accept omitting the analogues, and my answer is yes if the citation says plainly that the physiology and active form made incretin therapy possible. I do not accept that this is a settled ruling on attribution, though, and I would not want it described that way in any public text.

responses.point: Perlmann would move from Mojsov only if the record showed her priority to be weaker than credited, and also lists the B004 and B041 alternatives in the order B004 first.
responses.response: Your condition for moving is reasonable and I would apply it symmetrically. Nothing in the supplied record shows Mojsov's priority to be weaker than credited, and nothing shows it to be stronger either, so that question does not decide between us. What decides it for me is the principle. I would also keep the alternatives as B041 then B004, not as you have them, because B041 has the larger demonstrated clinical effect, although I accept your point that B004 has the cleaner two-person credit. If B007 stalled, I would need the committee to resolve the Eshhar originator question before a three-person B041 could be defended, and I would not claim that dropping Rosenberg resolves it.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1 peptide holds against Habener and others who are not on the supplied list. I cannot verify this from the record, and my ballot does not assume it is settled.

Whether the physiology-over-development principle is the right one, given how much of the clinical effect depends on long-acting acylated analogues. I am moving on a judgement about what the prize is for, and a reasonable member could weigh it the other way.
For B041, whether the unresolved Eshhar originator question makes any three-person configuration unsafe, including a June and Sadelain pair.
Whether long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy in obesity will change how the achievement should be described.
statement.conflict_note: No new disclosure since round 1. I have documented co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen on single-cell work, and my postdoctoral RNA-processing work was in Christopher Burge's group at MIT; none of this touches a credited name on B007, B041 or B004, and none is a formal mentor or supervisory tie. My field is close to B008 (antisense correction of SMN2 splicing), which is not in my configuration or alternatives. Linnarsson's and my co-authorship is disclosed on both sides and does not involve any credited person, so I do not consider recusal necessary.
